lesson.title: Inside a clause

steps.headline: A clause is a finite verb and its subject, and you start with the verb.

lead.text: A finite verb is the one that changes with time: chases, chased. Ask who or what does it and you have the subject. Together they make a clause. Poetry often reorders its words, so find the verb first.
Sonnet 18 reorders its words, so position will not help you. Go by tense: which word would change if the line moved into the past?

reveal.text: You tested for tense. “Declines” becomes “declined”, so it is the verb. Ask who or what declines: “every fair” is the subject.

steps.headline: Is the last part of “The storm shook the roof” and of “The storm was fierce” an object or a complement?

lead.text: Some verbs pass their action on to a thing. Others only link the subject to a description.

workedSteps.text: Find the verb and subject in each: “the storm shook” and “the storm was”.
“Shook” acts on something: “the roof” receives the action, so it is an object.
“Was” only links the subject to what follows: “fierce” says what the storm is like, so it is a complement.

reveal.text: You stripped the phrase back to its core. Every object is a phrase built round one noun, and the other words describe it.

steps.headline: Find the head noun of the object in “Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May”.

workedSteps.text: Find the verb and its subject: “do shake” and “rough winds”.
Ask what the winds shake: “the darling buds of May”. That whole phrase is the object.
Take away the describing words and keep the one noun they describe.

lead.text: A clause with its own subject and verb can still fail to stand alone. A subordinator such as “when”, “because” or “which” makes it lean on another clause. Sonnet 130, line 3: “If snow be white, why then her breasts are dun.”

reveal.text: The little word at the front decided it. Independent clauses make sense alone; dependent ones wait for the rest.

parts.text: in disgrace with fortune and men's eyes

lead.text: Each clause has its own finite verb, so counting finite verbs counts clauses. Infinitives such as “to serve” and participles such as “despising” carry no tense and do not count.

reveal.text: You counted one verb for each clause. In long poetic sentences, that is the fastest way to see how the thought is built.

lesson.orientation: Find the finite verb and its subject, tell an object from a complement, and separate independent clauses from dependent ones.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh text after a delay.

blocks.text: You say “The dog chases the ball”, then decide to tell it as yesterday's story.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the verb and subject in a line of verse, and tell whether a clause can stand alone.

recap.keyIdea: Find the finite verb first, then its subject. What follows is an object or a complement, and a clause opening with “if” or “when” cannot stand alone.

blocks.text: You found “declines” as the verb in a Shakespeare line. Then you picked “buds” as the head of an object and counted the finite verbs in Sonnet 116.

recap.nextHook: Two clauses can be joined well or badly. Next: which mark to put between them.

questions.prompt: Shakespeare's Sonnet 18 says 'And every fair from fair sometime declines.' Which single word is the finite verb?
hints: Put the line into the past tense. Which word changes form?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Declines' is the finite verb: it carries tense and would become 'declined' in the past. Its subject is 'every fair'.

questions.onCorrect: “Declines” is the verb: it would become “declined” in the past. Its subject is “every fair”.

misconceptions.feedback: That word names the subject or places the action. Put the line into the past and see which word has to change.

questions.prompt: In 'Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May', the object is a noun phrase. What is its head noun, the one word the rest of the phrase describes?
hints: Strip away the describing words. Which noun is left as the thing being shaken?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The object is 'the darling buds of May'; its head noun is 'buds'. 'Darling' and 'of May' modify it.

questions.onCorrect: The head of “the darling buds of May” is “buds”. “Darling” and “of May” only describe it.

misconceptions.feedback: “Darling” describes the noun. Find the noun that the other words are describing.
“May” sits inside “of May”, which describes the thing shaken rather than naming it.

questions.prompt: Sonnet 130 has 'If snow be white, why then her breasts are dun.' Which word makes the first clause dependent?
hints: Which word turns a statement into a condition?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'If' subordinates 'snow be white', so that clause cannot stand alone; 'her breasts are dun' can.

questions.onCorrect: “If” turns “snow be white” into a condition, so that clause cannot stand alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is part of the clause's own content. Look for the small word in front that makes it wait for an answer.

questions.prompt: How many finite verbs are in 'Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds'?
hints: A finite verb carries tense: test each word by putting the lines into the past.
Check the main clause, then the clause opened by 'which', then the clause opened by 'when'.
List one verb from each clause and count the list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: 'is', 'alters' and 'finds'. Each anchors a clause.

questions.onCorrect: Three: “is”, “alters” and “finds”. Each finite verb anchors its own clause.

misconceptions.feedback: Two clauses are easy to see, but the clause opened by “when” has a verb of its own.
That counts only the main clause. The clauses opened by “which” and “when” each have a verb.
Check that every word you counted carries tense. A noun is not a verb.

questions.prompt: Douglass, 1852: 'You may rejoice, I must mourn.' How many independent clauses does this sentence hold?
hints: Find each subject and finite verb pair.
Ask whether each clause could stand as a sentence on its own.
Neither clause opens with a subordinator.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: 'You may rejoice' and 'I must mourn'. Each could stand alone, and the comma between them is a deliberate splice.

questions.onCorrect: Two: “You may rejoice” and “I must mourn”. Each has its own subject and verb and could stand alone.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a second subject with its own verb. A comma does not fuse two clauses into one.
Pair each subject with its finite verb. “May” and “must” belong to the verbs beside them.

questions.prompt: In Lincoln's 'The world will little note, nor long remember what we say here', what is the grammatical function of 'what we say here'?
hints: Ask: the world will little note what? The answer names the object.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'What we say here' is a noun clause that receives the action of 'note' and 'remember', so it is their object. The subject is 'the world'.

questions.onCorrect: “What we say here” is what the world will note and remember, so it is the object of both verbs.

misconceptions.feedback: The subject does the noting. Ask what is noted: that is the clause in question.
A complement follows a linking verb and describes the subject. “Note” and “remember” act on something.

questions.prompt: Put “The dog chases the ball” into yesterday. Which word has to change?
hints: Say it aloud with “yesterday” at the start.
questions.onCorrect: “Chases” becomes “chased”. The word that changes with time is the one that holds the clause together.

misconceptions.feedback: “The” stays the same in any tense. Say the sentence with “yesterday” in front and listen for the word that shifts.
A noun keeps its form when the time changes. Look for the word that describes what happens.

questions.prompt: Which word is the finite verb in “The old man walked home slowly”?
hints: Put the sentence into the present. Which word changes?
questions.onCorrect: “Walked” carries the tense. It would be “walks” in the present, and “the old man” is who does it.

misconceptions.feedback: “Old” describes the man and does not change with time. Find the word that would change in the present.
“Slowly” describes how he walked. It stays the same in any tense.

questions.prompt: Why is “fierce” a complement and not an object?

acceptedIdeas: It says what the subject is like, and nothing receives an action.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “Was” links the subject to a description, so “fierce” is a complement.

choices.label: It says what the subject is like, and nothing receives an action.
It is the last word in the clause.
It is a single word, and objects need two.

questions.onCorrect: A complement says what the subject is or is like. An object receives the verb's action.

misconceptions.feedback: Position is not the test. Ask whether the word receives an action or describes the subject.
Objects can be one word too, as in “shook the roof”. Ask what the word does.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a dependent clause?
hints: Which one would leave you waiting for the rest of the sentence?

choices.label: The rain stopped and the sun came out

questions.onCorrect: “When” makes the clause lean on another one. It has a subject and a verb but cannot stand alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That could be a sentence on its own, so it is independent.
Both clauses here could stand alone. Look for a clause that opens with a word that makes it wait for more.

questions.prompt: “The dog chases the ball.” Retell it as yesterday's story. How many of its five words change?
hints: Say the sentence with “yesterday” at the start.
Change each word in turn and see which one you have to alter.
Nouns and “the” do not change with time.
questions.onCorrect: Only “chases” changes, to “chased”. The word that shifts with time is the one that holds the clause together.

misconceptions.feedback: Say it with “yesterday” in front. One of the words has to change.
Nouns and articles keep their form. Only the word for what happens shifts.
Most words stay put when the time changes. Test them one at a time.
